Summarise measurements

Source: vignettes/summary-statistics.Rmd
summary-statistics.Rmd

After counting satisfaction, the coordinator asks about assessment scores and income. summ() gives a first look at measurements; tabstat() makes a compact table of means. Both fit into dplyr pipelines and return results you can reuse.

Start with meaningful measurements

Here are the same twelve participants from Getting started, with income already cleaned and the two assessment items retained. Income is monthly; scores run from 0 to 10.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~income, ~score1, ~score2,
    1, "Riverside",    1200,       2,       4,
    2, "Riverside",    1500,       4,      NA,
    3, "Riverside",      NA,      NA,      NA,
    4, "Riverside",      NA,       6,       8,
    5, "Riverside",    2200,       8,      10,
    6, "Riverside",    1800,       4,       6,
    7, "Hilltop",      1400,       3,       5,
    8, "Hilltop",      2100,       5,       7,
    9, "Hilltop",      2600,       7,       9,
   10, "Hilltop",        NA,       9,      NA,
   11, "Hilltop",      2300,      NA,       8,
   12, "Hilltop",      1700,       6,       8
)

survey |> summ(income, starts_with("score"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 8
#>   name   type      n unique   min    mean     sd   max
#>   <chr>  <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 income dbl       9      9  1200 1867.   464.    2600
#> 2 score1 dbl      10      8     2    5.4    2.22     9
#> 3 score2 dbl       9      7     4    7.22   1.92    10

The default columns show observed counts, distinct values, minimum, mean, sample standard deviation and maximum. The selected measurements have different observed counts because missingness differs across items. We leave out id: being stored as a number does not make a column a measurement.

Ask for just the statistics you need

If the question is simply how average scores compare, start with tabstat():

survey |> tabstat(starts_with("score"), .by = centre)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   centre    name   type   mean
#>   <chr>     <chr>  <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   score1 dbl     6  
#> 2 Hilltop   score2 dbl     7.4
#> 3 Riverside score1 dbl     4.8
#> 4 Riverside score2 dbl     7

It uses the same calculations as summ(), but reports only the mean by default. For a reporting table, choose statistics and their order explicitly:

survey |>
  summ(income, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "median", "sd"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   centre    type      n  mean median    sd
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       5  2020   2100  476.
#> 2 Riverside dbl       4  1675   1650  427.

Missing measured values are omitted from each calculation. sd uses the sample denominator, and undefined statistics are NA, for example an SD based on one observation. Use .detail = TRUE to explore the full supported set; .stat takes precedence when you supply it.

For completeness, ask for counts and the observed proportion together:

survey |>
  summ(starts_with("score"), .stat = c("n", "miss_n", "valid_pct", "mean"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   name   type      n miss_n valid_pct  mean
#>   <chr>  <chr> <int>  <int>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 score1 dbl      10      2     0.833  5.4 
#> 2 score2 dbl       9      3     0.75   7.22

miss_n (also called missing) counts missing measurements. valid_pct is a 0-1 proportion, unlike the 0-100 percentages from tab().

Calculate first, then summarise

Named expressions can create a column for this summary without changing the source tibble:

survey |> summ(income_thousands = income / 1000, .by = centre)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   centre    type      n unique   min  mean    sd   max
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int>  <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       5      5   1.4  2.02 0.476   2.6
#> 2 Riverside dbl       4      4   1.2  1.68 0.427   2.2

For a measurement that you will reuse, create it in mutate(). The row average uses whichever assessment items are observed; it stays missing when neither is.

scored <- survey |>
  mutate(score = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)))

scored |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd")) |>
  arrange(desc(mean))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   centre    type      n  mean    sd
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       6   7    1.79
#> 2 Riverside dbl       5   5.6  2.41

The centre comparison now uses one score per participant. An explicit .name = TRUE retains a name column even when summarising a single variable.

Make grouping choices explicit

summ() and tabstat() inherit group_by() groups, or accept .by for one operation. Their results are ungrouped. An explicit .by replaces inherited groups. Computed expressions inside summ() are evaluated before grouping; use grouped mutate() first for calculations that depend on each group’s values.

Suppose participant 12’s centre was not recorded. Keep that participant’s measurement visible as a separate group:

unknown_centre <- scored |>
  mutate(centre = if_else(id == 12, NA_character_, centre))

unknown_centre |> summ(score, .by = centre, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   centre    type      n  mean
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       5   7  
#> 2 Riverside dbl       5   5.6
#> 3 NA        dbl       1   7

Use .missing = FALSE to exclude missing grouping keys:

unknown_centre |>
  summ(score, .by = centre, .missing = FALSE, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   centre    type      n  mean
#>   <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   dbl       5   7  
#> 2 Riverside dbl       5   5.6

That option does not change how missing measurements are handled.

Read percentiles using Stata’s rule

Percentiles are useful when a mean hides a wide income distribution. Request median, q1, q3, or percentiles such as p10 and p90:

survey |> summ(income, .stat = c("n", "p10", "q1", "median", "q3", "p90"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   type      n   p10    q1 median    q3   p90
#>   <chr> <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 dbl       9  1200  1500   1800  2200  2600

These follow Stata’s percentile rule, which can differ from R’s default quantile(). A small example makes the difference visible:

tibble(score = 1:4) |> summ(score, .stat = c("p25", "p50", "p75"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   type    p25   p50   p75
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 int     1.5   2.5   3.5

The quartiles are 1.5 and 3.5. For percentile-rank columns, use dplyr::percent_rank(); for quantile groups, use xtile(). pc() instead calculates each value’s percentage of a total.

Distinguish frequency and analytic weights

Suppose an aggregate register has three score values and their frequencies. Frequency weights reproduce the expanded participants:

register <- tribble(
  ~score, ~people,
       2,       3,
       6,       1,
      10,       1
)

register |>
  summ(score, .wt = people, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd", "p50"))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   type      n  mean    sd   p50
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 dbl       5   4.4  3.58     2

The reported n is five. Analytic weights rescale to the observed row count within each variable and group, changing the reported count and sample SD:

register |>
  summ(
    score, .wt = people, .wt_type = "analytic",
    .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd")
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   type      n  mean    sd
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 dbl       3   4.4  3.92

The mean agrees, but n is now three. Weights must be finite and nonnegative; missing weights exclude rows with a message. These are descriptive weighting rules, not design-based standard errors for a complex survey.

Choose a convenient return form

Numeric and calendar variables have different units, so the default separates their summaries into a list when both families occur. Request .type = "tibble" when you need one combined table:

visits <- tibble(
  score = c(4, 8),
  day = readr::parse_date(c("2026-09-01", "2026-09-03"))
)

visits |> summ(.type = "tibble", .stat = c("n", "min", "mean", "max"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   name  type      n min        mean       max       
#>   <chr> <chr> <int> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>     
#> 1 score dbl       2 4          6          8         
#> 2 day   date      2 2026-09-01 2026-09-02 2026-09-03

Shared location columns become character so they can hold numbers and dates. The default separate tables preserve each family’s statistic types. See the conventions guide for calendar spread units and container preservation.

Unsupported non-numeric columns are omitted with a message. .keep_all = TRUE keeps them for counts and distinct values. Labelled numeric variables use their codes; factors use level codes and produce a message. Select meaningful measurements instead of averaging category codes. Entirely missing columns still warn and remain with n = 0 and NA statistics, including sum; .drop_empty = TRUE omits those rows.

Look at relationships next

Do income and the two assessment items move together? corr() uses one common complete sample across all selected columns:

survey |> corr(income, score1, score2)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   var1   var2       r     n
#>   <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>
#> 1 income score1 0.847     7
#> 2 income score2 0.847     7
#> 3 score1 score2 1         7

pwcorr() instead uses the available observations for each pair, reporting counts and p-values:

survey |> pwcorr(income, score1, score2)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   var1   var2       r     n        p
#>   <chr>  <chr>  <dbl> <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 income score1 0.850     8 7.47e- 3
#> 2 income score2 0.845     8 8.25e- 3
#> 3 score1 score2 1         8 2.74e-47

Compare the n columns: changing the missing-data rule changes which participants contribute. pwcorr(.listwise = TRUE) uses a common sample. spearman() computes rank correlations on a common sample by default, with .pairwise = TRUE for pairwise samples. The tiny survey illustrates the interfaces, not evidence about programme effects. See the correlation reference for additional options.

Return to data preparation to build measurements, or use category tables for responses that are categories.
